title: The Hearing Before the Job: How Senate Confirmation Works
hook: Cabinet secretaries don't just get appointed — the Senate gets a vote first. A contentious July 2026 hearing for the next attorney general shows the confirmation gauntlet at work.
key_points: The Constitution's 'advice and consent' clause requires Senate confirmation for Cabinet officials, federal judges, and many other top posts.
A nominee testifies at a public committee hearing, where senators question their record, before a floor vote decides confirmation.
In July 2026, Acting AG Todd Blanche — already confirmed once as the Justice Department's No. 2 official — faced a second, more contentious hearing to become permanent attorney general.
The same week, a separate Senate committee held its own confirmation hearing for a CDC director nominee, showing how many agencies cycle through this same process.
A hearing lets senators who lack the votes to block a nominee still question them publicly and put objections on the record.
content_html: Getting a job as a Cabinet secretary, federal judge, or other senior official isn't just a presidential decision. The Constitution's "advice and consent" clause hands the Senate a check on that power: a nominee doesn't take office until senators have had their say and voted to confirm.
extra_html: In practice, that means a public hearing before the relevant committee, where senators — from both parties — question the nominee's record, positions, and fitness for the job, before a committee vote and then a full Senate floor vote. NPR's Ryan Lucas reported that Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche faced exactly this in July 2026: already confirmed once, as the Justice Department's No. 2 official, he returned to Capitol Hill for a second, more contentious hearing seeking the top job on a permanent basis. The same week, a separate Senate committee ran a CDC director nominee through the identical process — a reminder that dozens of top posts across the government cycle through this same gauntlet, often in parallel. Even senators who lack the votes to block a nominee still get something from the hearing: a public, on-the-record chance to press them on positions and past conduct, which is part of why these sessions can turn contentious regardless of the outcome.

flashcards.prompt: What does the Constitution's 'advice and consent' clause require before a Cabinet nominee can take office?
flashcards.back_html: Senate confirmation — a majority floor vote, usually after a public committee hearing where senators question the nominee's fitness and record.

flashcards.prompt: Why did Todd Blanche face a Senate hearing in July 2026 even though he'd already been confirmed once?

choices.text: He was nominated for a different, higher post — permanent attorney general, not deputy AG
The Senate requires every official to be reconfirmed each year
His first confirmation had been ruled invalid by a court

flashcards.explanation_html: Each distinct Senate-confirmed position requires its own confirmation, even for someone already serving in a related role.

flashcards.prompt: What can a confirmation hearing let senators do, even without the votes to block a nominee?

choices.text: Publicly question the nominee and put their objections on the record
Automatically postpone the floor vote indefinitely
Force the nominee to withdraw on the spot

flashcards.explanation_html: The hearing itself has value as public accountability — a recorded, on-camera chance to press a nominee — separate from whether the vote to confirm ultimately succeeds.
